clue.text: Daily thesis

definitions.meaning: a daily is a newspaper published every day
a thesis is a scholarly essay or dissertation, a written study

explanation.definitionFit: A daily is a newspaper, and an academic essay or study read to a learned society is also so called.

clue.text: Hodgson, say, who does not need full lunch yet?

definitions.text: Hodgson, say, who does not need full lunch yet?

parts.words: Hodgson, say, who does not need full lunch yet
parts.note: a farm lad is not yet a grown man, so he would not need the full ploughman's lunch of bread, cheese and pickle

explanation.surface: A man called Hodgson is not yet hungry enough for a full midday meal.
explanation.walkthrough: A ploughman's lunch is a British pub meal of bread, cheese and pickle; the boy who works the plough is not yet a ploughman, so he wants less than the full one. Hodgson is offered as a sample name for such a lad.
explanation.definitionFit: A young farm worker who leads the team that tills the fields.

clue.text: Scotsman in post office has all the keys

definitions.note: a description: the instrument has a full keyboard

indicators.note: the Scotsman's name sits in the abbreviation for post office

parts.note: Ian is a typically Scottish man's name

explanation.surface: A Scot working in the post office holds every key to the building.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints 'has all'; the stray apostrophe is an OCR slip.
explanation.definitionFit: A keyboard instrument has a whole row of black and white keys covering every note.

clue.text: One who would not keep sovereigns?

definitions.text: One who would not keep sovereigns?

parts.words: One who would not keep sovereigns
parts.note: sovereigns read as monarchs rather than gold coins, and keep as keep alive rather than save

explanation.surface: A spendthrift who cannot hold on to his gold coins.
explanation.walkthrough: Sovereigns look like old British gold coins, so the clue seems to be about a spendthrift; read them as kings and queens, and not keeping them alive makes a killer of monarchs.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who murders a king, or the crime of king-killing itself.

clue.text: Kaos, for example, a stagnant place

parts.note: the word is SOAK, which means water, written back to front, so it is water read backwards

explanation.surface: A Greek island held up as an example of a sleepy, out-of-the-way spot.
explanation.walkthrough: Kaos looks like a Greek place name, but it is SOAK spelt backwards; soak means water, so the answer read as wordplay, 'back water', describes the clue word.
explanation.definitionFit: A backwater is a quiet, isolated place untouched by progress, like still water off the main stream.

clue.text: Home fixture for City

definitions.meaning: a fitting in a house: the tub you wash in
a city in Somerset, England, famous for its Roman spa

explanation.surface: A football fixture played at home by a team called City.
explanation.walkthrough: Fixture and City suggest a football match, but one is a fitted tub and the other the English spa city.
explanation.definitionFit: A tub plumbed into a house is a fixed fitting; the Somerset spa town is also a city.

clue.text: Pole Star-gazer?

definitions.meaning: an astronomer, someone who studies the heavens

explanation.surface: Someone gazing at the Pole Star.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole Star' reads as the north star, but split it: a Pole (a man from Poland) and a star-gazer, the astronomer who put the sun at the centre.
explanation.definitionFit: The Renaissance astronomer was Polish, and his life's work was watching and modelling the heavens.

clue.text: Pop figure in the City Road

definitions.text: Pop figure in the City Road

parts.words: Pop figure in the City Road
parts.note: the nursery rhyme runs 'Up and down the City Road, in and out the Eagle, that's the way the money goes, pop goes the' animal

explanation.surface: A pop star seen walking along a London street.
explanation.walkthrough: Pop figure suggests a pop star, but it is the animal that goes 'pop' in the old London rhyme set on City Road; 'pop' there is slang for pawning.
explanation.definitionFit: The small mustelid of the rhyme, a slender predator related to the stoat.

clue.text: Inner gate conceals mandarin

indicators.note: the letters of inner gate hide the fruit in a jumbled form, so they must be rearranged to reveal it

explanation.surface: An inner gate of the palace hides a Chinese official.
explanation.walkthrough: Mandarin looks like a Chinese official behind the palace gate, but it is the citrus fruit; 'conceals' asks you to rearrange INNER GATE.
explanation.definitionFit: A mandarin is a small loose-skinned orange, and this fruit is one variety of it.

clue.text: Rugby hovel of antiquated appearance

parts.note: RU stands for Rugby Union
a sty is a filthy hut, a pigsty or hovel

explanation.surface: A tumbledown shack at a rugby ground looks very old.
explanation.definitionFit: Something rusty is corroded and worn with age, so it looks old and neglected.

clue.text: Extremely colourful butterfly

parts.note: extremely read as at the extremity: the insect's wing ends are coloured a bright shade

explanation.surface: A gaudy butterfly in vivid colours.
explanation.walkthrough: Extremely seems to intensify colourful, but it means at the extremity: the wing tips are coloured, and the colour is a bright one.
explanation.definitionFit: A common European butterfly whose male has bright tips on its white forewings.

clue.text: Child martyr has silver head almost

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

indicators.note: the headland word loses its final letter, so it is nearly complete

parts.note: a ness is a headland, as in Loch Ness or Dungeness

explanation.surface: A young martyr whose hair has turned nearly silver.
explanation.walkthrough: Head is not a person's head but a ness, a promontory; 'almost' drops its last S.
explanation.definitionFit: Saint of that name was a Roman girl of about twelve put to death for her faith.

clue.text: Grievance of Marx duck's off

indicators.note: the duck has gone away from the comedian's name

parts.note: Groucho is the most famous of the Marx Brothers
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, so the letter O

explanation.surface: A complaint that Marx's duck has gone missing.
explanation.walkthrough: A duck is a zero score in cricket, giving O.
explanation.definitionFit: A grouch can be a sulky complaint or fit of grumbling as well as the person making it.

clue.text: "——— —yallery, Grosvenor Gallery" (Patience)

parts.note: the missing word completes a line from Gilbert and Sullivan's comic opera Patience mocking the aesthetes

explanation.surface: A quotation with a gap, taken from a comic opera.
explanation.walkthrough: Patience is a Gilbert and Sullivan operetta satirising the aesthetic movement; Bunthorne is a 'greenery-yallery, Grosvenor Gallery, foot-in-the-grave young man'. The OCR misread 'yallery' as 'gallery'.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is a fill-in from the lyric, describing the greens and yellows of aesthetic taste; on its own it means foliage.

clue.text: "Conduct forward"- Peggotty's opinion of him

parts.note: to conduct a vehicle or party is to steer it
forth means onward or forward

explanation.surface: A Dickens character sums up a man as one who led someone astray.
explanation.walkthrough: In Dickens's David Copperfield the fisherman Peggotty's niece Emily is led off by this charming cad, so 'conduct forward' is the family's verdict on him.
explanation.definitionFit: The 'him' is the seducer in Dickens's novel whom Peggotty's family come to curse.

clue.text: Colourful clue to one not so bald as made out

indicators.note: made out suggests claimed, but here the letters are made into something else, reshaped

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: A hint that somebody is less bald than people claim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made out' rearranges I plus NOTSOBALD. A detective's clue that is red in colour is a mark of blood.
explanation.definitionFit: A mark of blood is a red trace that a detective treats as evidence.

clue.text: Cricket side gets permission for a bar

parts.note: on, or leg, is the half of a cricket field behind the batsman's legs
a licence is formal permission

explanation.surface: A cricket team is allowed to open its own bar.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the on side is the leg side. In Britain an off-licence is a shop selling drink to take away; this is the opposite, a place licensed for drinking on the premises.
explanation.definitionFit: A pub or bar licensed to serve alcohol to be drunk on site is known by this term in Britain.

clue.text: Compact stable

explanation.surface: A small horse's stall.
explanation.walkthrough: Compact and stable look like nouns (a powder case, a horse's home) but both are adjectives here.
explanation.definitionFit: Something solid and dense is unyielding; something steady and fixed is also so described.

clue.text: Common sense that is worth time developing

indicators.note: developing means growing into a new form, so the letters of worth and time are reshaped

explanation.surface: Practical wisdom is worth the time it takes to acquire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'developing' rearranges WORTH TIME.
explanation.definitionFit: Native wit or practical shrewdness that one is born with rather than taught.

clue.text: Disciple has to stick to holy writ

parts.note: to adhere is to stick fast
NT is the New Testament, part of holy scripture

explanation.surface: A follower must stick closely to the scriptures.
explanation.definitionFit: A follower or supporter of a leader, faith or cause.

clue.text: It holds the key to Open University

definitions.text: It holds the key to Open University

parts.words: It holds the key to Open University
parts.note: a lock that a key opens shares its name with an American Ivy League university

explanation.surface: Something essential to Britain's distance-learning university.
explanation.walkthrough: The Open University is Britain's distance-learning university, but here 'open' is a verb: the cylinder lock bearing this name holds a key, and the name is also an American university.
explanation.definitionFit: A cylinder lock maker's brand name, which is also the Ivy League college in Connecticut.

clue.text: The gin's due to be drunk, bless you!

indicators.note: drunk suggests something tipsy and staggering, so the letters reel into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone toasts the gin owed to them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be drunk' rearranges THE GINS DUE.
explanation.definitionFit: A German word for health, said after somebody sneezes in the same way English speakers wish them well.

clue.text: French rouge?

parts.note: rouge is French for red, and the red wine of Bordeaux is a French red

explanation.surface: Make-up from France.
explanation.walkthrough: Rouge looks like make-up, but read in French it means red: a red wine of France.
explanation.definitionFit: The British name for the red wines of the Bordeaux region.

clue.text: A features-editor's work, reducing the number of lines?

definitions.text: A features-editor's work, reducing the number of lines?

parts.words: A features-editor's work, reducing the number of lines
parts.note: features read as the parts of a face, and lines as wrinkles rather than lines of print

explanation.surface: A newspaper features editor cuts copy to fit the page.
explanation.walkthrough: A features editor seems to cut lines of print, but the features are facial and the lines are wrinkles a cosmetic surgeon smooths away.
explanation.definitionFit: Cosmetic surgery tightening the skin of the face to remove wrinkles.

clue.text: Novel source of mill-power

parts.note: the river driving the mill in George Eliot's novel The Mill on the river of this name

explanation.surface: An innovative way to power a mill.
explanation.walkthrough: Novel seems to mean new, but it is the book: George Eliot's The Mill on the ___, whose river turns the mill.
explanation.definitionFit: The river that runs past Dorlcote Mill in George Eliot's novel.

clue.text: Decline junk

definitions.meaning: to turn down or say no

explanation.surface: A drop in the value of junk.
explanation.walkthrough: As a verb it is stressed on the second syllable, as a noun on the first.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn something down is to reject it; rubbish thrown away is also so called.

clue.text: Houseman in a state of collapse?

definitions.text: Houseman in a state of collapse?

parts.words: Houseman in a state of collapse
parts.note: Poe's story The Fall of the House of this name ends with the mansion collapsing

explanation.surface: A junior hospital doctor on the point of exhaustion.
explanation.walkthrough: A houseman is a junior hospital doctor in Britain, but here he is the man of the house in Poe's tale, which ends as the house falls.
explanation.definitionFit: Roderick, head of the family in Poe's tale, whose house crumbles; the name also means a doorkeeper.

clue.text: Nibble prune

definitions.meaning: to graze or bite off short, as sheep do grass

explanation.surface: Biting into a dried plum.
explanation.walkthrough: Prune looks like the dried plum, but it is the verb to trim.
explanation.definitionFit: Grazing animals bite grass short, and gardeners trim hedges short: both are this verb.

clue.text: He has a Sam Browne — real leather piece of equipment

indicators.note: only a piece of the run of letters across Browne and real is wanted

explanation.surface: A soldier owns a Sam Browne, a genuine leather belt.
explanation.walkthrough: A Sam Browne is a military leather belt with a shoulder strap. The letters sit across 'Browne real'.
explanation.definitionFit: A possessor is the one who has something, so 'he has' describes the possessor.

clue.text: Take a box for this raw English revue

parts.note: rare meat is barely cooked, almost raw
a revue is a theatrical show

explanation.surface: Book a theatre box for a crude English variety show.
explanation.walkthrough: A box sounds like a theatre box, but this old street entertainment was a peep show carried in a box.
explanation.definitionFit: A travelling peep show whose pictures were viewed through a hole in a portable box.

clue.text: Factory where little bread is made.

definitions.text: Factory where little bread is made

parts.words: Factory where little bread is made
parts.note: bread is slang for money, so it is a works where the pay is tiny, not a bakery

explanation.surface: A small bakery.
explanation.walkthrough: Bread suggests a bakery, but it is slang for money: workers in this factory earn very little.
explanation.definitionFit: A workplace where labourers toil long hours for low wages in poor conditions.

clue.text: Pitch old books and cards

parts.note: pitch is a black tarry substance
OT is the Old Testament, the older books of the Bible

explanation.surface: Throwing away old books and playing cards.
explanation.definitionFit: A pack of picture cards used for fortune-telling or for a card game.
